title: I Gave My Last $40 to a Homeless Woman Outside a Pharmacy. The Next Morning, She Was Waiting at My Job Interview (PART 2)

blocks.text: …she lost her job for doing the right thing."
Her name was Dr. Margaret Lowell. Twenty-six years ago, in 2000, she was an attending physician at a hospital in Boston. My mother was a night nurse on her floor. I was a baby.

That year, the hospital started using a new brand of infusion pump, the machines that deliver medicine through an IV. My mother noticed something wrong. Twice in one week, a pump delivered far more medication than it was set to give. She caught both errors in time. She reported them. The hospital's administrators told her the pumps had been tested and to stop making trouble.
She refused to use them on her patients. She was written up, then suspended, then let go.
"I was the only doctor who backed her," Dr. Lowell said. "I filed my own report with the FDA.
Four months later, the manufacturer recalled every one of those pumps nationwide. Your mother's reports were the first in the file."
My mother never told me. She worked at a nursing home for the rest of her career. I always thought she'd just preferred it.

The company that made those pumps doesn't exist anymore. Years later, it was bought by the company I was interviewing with. When the new owners reviewed the old recall files, they found my mother's name. They created a patient safety award in her honor. They'd been trying to find her.

Dr. Lowell sits on the company's ethics board and sometimes helps with hiring. When she saw my emergency contact on my resume, she recognized the name immediately. She'd asked for my interview herself.
She didn't know until the conference room door opened that I was the stranger who'd given her my last $40 the night before.
"Your mother would have done the same thing," she said.

I got the job. It wasn't because of my mother. Dr. Lowell made sure I went through the same interviews as everyone else. But at the end of my first week, the company held a small ceremony to present my mother with the safety award that carries her name.
My mother cried. She hugged Dr. Lowell for a long time. Then she said, "I always wondered if anyone remembered."
